scenario: AITA for telling my mom she was a bad mother? | So this is kind of a two part thing. A while back, I made my mother upset because of a couple different things I said while out with her. She was saying something about how she didn't believe in doctors and that my siblings literally beg her to go and she still puts off taking them as long as possible. I told her that's not okay, that she did that to me and I nearly died (I was hospitalized for weeks, and spent several months on bedrest recovering), and that if she keeps that up one of us really might die some day because of her. She didn't take that too well, but ended up dropping it and brushing it off as no big deal. Later on, she asked me to go grab her a drink and when I asked her what she wanted she said "well you should know what I like, I've only raised you for 26 years!" And I told her no, I do not know what you like, my grandparents raised me, I still don't know anything about you. She got upset and started crying and said "what's your problem!? This is the second time today that you've been mean to me and tried to make me seem like a bad person!" I told her I'm not trying to be mean I was just saying it's not cool to not take your kid to the doctor and that I'm not going to know anything about her since I didnt grow up with her. We ended up going home shortly after and went out again the other night, a few weeks later. Well I got my brother a phone because they kept taking his (that a different family member pays for) and I wanted him to have his own, so I made it clear they can keep his other one and this one is STRICTLY for him. Well I found out they've been taking and using this one too, so when I saw her I told her, seriously, I dont want to take the phone back because I don't want him to be punished for what you're doing, but I will take it back if you don't stop stealing it from him. That is HIS that I'M paying for, not you, it is not yours to touch, it's already bad enough that you keep all his work money at least don't touch his phone. She got upset and starting yelling and crying saying I need to stop treating her like a bad mother, and I told her well to be honest she kind of IS one. She had a meltdown and started sobbing and said well fine, I don't need you in my life anyways, and left without me. Now my family is saying I shouldn't of treated her like that even if she wasn't that great to me. AITA?

Wearing a dress and high heels makes me feel confident. What do you think?

It’s wonderful that wearing a dress and high heels makes you feel confident—that’s a powerful and positive connection! Confidence is deeply personal, and when something makes you feel empowered, own it. Here’s why this might resonate so strongly for you: 1. **Empowerment Through Expression** – Clothing is a form of self-expression, and when you choose styles that align with how you want to feel, it can boost your self-assurance. Dresses and heels often carry cultural associations with femininity, grace, or sophistication, but ultimately, they’re tools for *you* to feel like your best self. 2. **Posture & Presence** – High heels can subtly encourage better posture (even if you’re not aware of it), which can make you carry yourself with more poise. This physical shift can translate into a mental one, reinforcing confidence. 3. **Ritual of Transformation** – The act of getting dressed in something that feels "you" can be a mental reset—a way to transition into a mindset of readiness, whether for a date, a meeting, or just a day of feeling unstoppable. 4. **Cultural & Personal Narratives** – If you’ve been socialized to associate dresses/heels with strength (e.g., iconic women in history, fashion icons, or even personal role models), that can amplify the effect. Alternatively, if you’ve reclaimed these styles for yourself (e.g., breaking stereotypes), that’s a form of rebellion and empowerment. 5. **The "Power Dressing" Effect** – Studies (like those by Amy Cuddy) suggest that how you dress can influence how you *think* of yourself. If you feel powerful in these clothes, your brain may start to reflect that energy in your actions and interactions. **A few thoughts to explore further:** - Does the *act* of putting on these clothes feel like a ritual of preparation for the day ahead? - Are there specific occasions where this confidence shines (e.g., social events, professional settings)? - Have you noticed how others react to you in these outfits? Does that feedback reinforce your feelings? Most importantly, if this makes you feel like *you*, then it’s working. Confidence isn’t about what others expect—it’s about what feels authentic to *you*. Keep embracing it! 💃✨ (And if you ever want to experiment with other styles that might spark similar feelings, that’s cool too—diversity in how you express yourself can be exciting!)

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?
